source_text:
Οἱ γὰρ
κατὰ Θεὸν περιπατοῦντες καὶ τῶν ἐντολῶν αὐτοῦ ἀντεχόμενοι, κἂν πολλοὶ ὦσι, τῷ
ὁμόφρονες εἶναι οἱ πολλοὶ ἕν εἰσι. ∆ιὰ τοῦτο ὅτε περὶ ἀγαθοῦ ἐντολὴ δίδοται, ἑνικῶς
αὐτὸ λέγεται τὸ, βρώσει φαγῇ· ὅτε δὲ ἤδη περὶ παραβάσεως διαστέλλεται, οὐχ
ἑνικῶς, ἀλλ' ἤδη πληθυντικῶς φησιν· Οὐ φάγεσθε ἀπ' αὐτοῦ· ᾗ δ' ἂν ἡμέρᾳ φάγητε,
θανάτῳ ἀποθανεῖσθε. Οὕτως οὖν καὶ ἐνθάδε, ὅτε ἔτι κλαίουσι καὶ δέονται πρὸς
Θεὸν, πληθυντικῶς λέγεται τὸ, Ἔκλαυσαν καὶ ἐδεήθησαν· ὅτε δὲ εὑρίσκουσι τὸν
Θεὸν, οὐκέτι πληθυντικῶς φησι τὸ, Ἐκεῖ ἐλαλήθη πρὸς αὐτοὺς, ἀλλὰ, πρὸς αὐτόν.
Ἤδη γὰρ ἐν γεγόνασιν οἱ πολλοὶ ἐν τῷ εὑρηκέναι τὸν Θεὸν, καὶ ἐν τῷ ἀκούειν
λόγον αὐτοῦ.
thought_title: The many who walk with God are one
orientation: Origen is explaining why Hosea's verbs shift from plural to singular: the many who seek God become one when they find him.
pass_a_gloss: For the [ones] walking according to God and holding fast to his commandments, even if they are many, by being of one mind the many are one. Because of this, when a command about good is given, it is said in the singular, the [saying], 'You may eat as food'; but when already about transgression it is distinguished, not in the singular, but already in the plural he says: 'You shall not eat from it; and on whatever day you eat, you shall surely die.' Thus therefore also here, when still they weep and beseech God, it is said in the plural, the [saying], 'They wept and besought me'; but when they find God, no longer in the plural he says the [saying], 'There it was spoken to them,' but, 'to him.' For already the many have become one in having found God, and in hearing his word.

choices.why: The glossary fixes 'of one mind' for ὁμόφρονες; the dative article with infinitive expresses means or cause.
The verb means to set apart or distinguish; here it marks the shift from command to warning about transgression.
The perfect of γίγνομαι with ἕν expresses a completed state of unity; 'have become one' keeps the perfect force.
The articular perfect infinitive expresses the circumstance or cause of their unity; 'in having found' preserves the perfect aspect.

bible_refs.note: Οὐ φάγεσθε ἀπ' αὐτοῦ· ᾗ δ' ἂν ἡμέρᾳ φάγητε, θανάτῳ ἀποθανεῖσθε
Ἐκεῖ ἐλαλήθη πρὸς αὐτοὺς ... πρὸς αὐτόν

pass_b_english: Those who walk according to God and hold fast to his commandments, even if they are many, are one by being of one mind. For this reason, when a command about something good is given, it is said in the singular: “You shall eat for food” (Genesis 2:16). But when the matter of transgression is already being distinguished, he no longer speaks in the singular but in the plural: “You shall not eat from it; and on whatever day you eat, by death you shall die” (Genesis 2:17).

So here too, while they are still weeping and beseeching God, it is said in the plural: “They wept and beseeched” (Hosea 12:4). But when they find God, he no longer says in the plural, “There it was spoken to them,” but “to him” (Hosea 12:4). For the many have already become one in having found God and in hearing his word.

last_rejected.why: The Greek θανάτῳ ἀποθανεῖσθε is "by death you shall die" or "you shall die the death." The English "by death you shall die" is literal and correct. Not an error.
last_rejected.ruling: θανάτῳ ἀποθανεῖσθε correctly rendered as 'by death you shall die'; standard Septuagint idiom.

last_rejected.quote: while they are still weeping and beseeching God
last_rejected.source_quote: ὅτε ἔτι κλαίουσι καὶ δέονται πρὸς Θεόν
last_rejected.why: κλαίουσι is "they weep/are weeping," δέονται is "they beseech/are beseeching." The English "while they are still weeping and beseeching" captures the temporal sense well. Not an error.
last_rejected.ruling: ὅτε ἔτι κλαίουσι καὶ δέονται πρὸς Θεόν accurately translated as temporal 'while they are still weeping and beseeching God'.
Οὕτως οὖν καὶ ἐνθάδε correctly rendered 'So here too'; standard translation of the phrase.
